etymology: From the Greek thronos tes charitos, “throne of grace,” the seat of God’s favour whereto the believer draws near through Christ the High Priest.
biblical_def: The throne of grace is the mercy-seat of God, opened to the believer through Jesus the great High Priest, whereto he may come with boldness in every time of need. The apostle, having shown that we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin (Heb 4:15), draws the conclusion: Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need (Heb 4:16). The dictionary marks this as the great access of the gospel. Under the law the high priest alone entered the holiest, and that but once a year, not without blood; but Christ, having obtained eternal redemption for us (Heb 9:12), hath consecrated a new and living way. So the throne which to the sinner out of Christ is a throne of judgment is, to the believer in Christ, a throne of grace. He comes not trembling as a stranger but boldly as a son, for the God who sitteth upon it hath given His Son to be the propitiation for sin. The mercy is obtained, the grace is found, the help is timely; for the High Priest at the right hand of it ever liveth to make intercession (Heb 7:25). So the Scripture teaches the saint to draw near with full assurance of faith, looking to no merit of his own but to the blood that opened the way.
webster_summary: The mercy-seat of God, opened to the believer through Christ the High Priest, whereto he comes boldly for mercy and grace.
webster_full: THRONE OF GRACE, the seat of God’s favour whereto the believer draws near through Christ.
It is the same throne which to the sinner out of Christ is a throne of judgment.
The believer comes boldly, not as a stranger but as a son.
There he obtains mercy, and finds grace to help in time of need.
The High Priest at the right hand of it ever liveth to make intercession.
scriptures: Heb 4:16

Heb 7:25

Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
corruption_summary: A glory of the gospel little redefined; it recovers the believer’s bold access to God through the one Mediator, Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The throne of grace has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a phrase of comfort upon many lips. The dictionary records it that the reader may know it not as a vague sentiment of divine kindness but as the definite access purchased by the blood of Christ and entered through Him alone.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is bold access to God through the one Mediator. The throne is grace only because Christ the High Priest hath opened it with His blood; apart from Him the same throne is a throne of judgment, and no man dare approach. So the saint is taught to come, not presuming upon a general benevolence, but pleading the finished work of the Son who ever liveth to intercede. The boldness is real, the mercy is sure, the grace is timely; and it is all of grace, that no flesh should glory in His presence.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “throne of grace,” the phrase names the mercy-seat opened to the believer through Christ.
roots_lines: Throne of Grace — Greek thronos tes charitos, “throne of grace.”
It is the mercy-seat of God opened through Christ the High Priest.
The believer comes boldly to it as a son, not a stranger.
There he obtains mercy and finds grace to help in time of need.
The interceding Christ stands at the right hand of it for ever.
usage: Come boldly unto the throne of grace, for the blood of Christ hath opened the way.
Let us obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
The throne that to the sinner is judgment is, to the believer in Christ, grace.

etymology: From the Greek haima rhantismou, “blood of sprinkling,” the atoning blood of Christ applied to the believer, which speaketh better things than that of Abel.
biblical_def: The blood of sprinkling is the atoning blood of Jesus Christ, shed upon the cross and applied to the believer’s conscience, which the apostle sets among the glories whereto the saints are come. Ye are come, he says, to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel (Heb 12:24). The dictionary marks the contrast. The blood of Abel, slain by his brother, cried from the ground for vengeance (Gen 4:10); but the blood of Christ speaketh better things, for it cries not for the sinner’s condemnation but for his pardon, pleading the price paid in full. So the believer is bidden to draw near with a true heart, having his heart sprinkled from an evil conscience (Heb 10:22). The figure is drawn from the old covenant, wherein almost all things were by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission (Heb 9:22). But the blood of bulls and of goats could not take away sins; it was the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself without spot to God, that purgeth the conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Heb 9:14). So the Scripture teaches that the sinner’s peace stands not upon his own amendment but upon the blood once shed and now sprinkled by the Spirit upon the heart, which silences the accusing law and conscience together, and speaks of mercy obtained and wrath removed.
webster_summary: The atoning blood of Christ applied to the believer’s conscience, which speaketh better things than the blood of Abel.
webster_full: BLOOD OF SPRINKLING, the atoning blood of Christ applied to the believer.
It is set in contrast to the blood of Abel, which cried for vengeance.
The blood of Christ speaketh better things, crying for pardon and peace.
By it the heart is sprinkled from an evil conscience.
It purgeth the conscience from dead works to serve the living God.
scriptures: And to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel.
Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
Heb 9:22
And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.
Heb 9:14
How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?
corruption_summary: A glory of the gospel little redefined; it recovers the once-shed blood of Christ as the only purger of the conscience.
corruption_paragraphs: The blood of sprinkling has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving in the hymns and the preaching of the church. The dictionary records it that the reader may hold fast the substitutionary blood of Christ as the ground of his peace, and not soften the figure into a mere emblem of self-giving love.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that without shedding of blood is no remission. The conscience is purged not by reformation but by the blood of Christ, who offered Himself without spot to God; and that blood, sprinkled upon the heart by the Spirit, speaketh better things than Abel’s, crying not for vengeance but for pardon. So the saint is taught to rest his assurance upon the price already paid, and to silence the accusing law and the accusing conscience alike by the plea of the blood once shed and now applied.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “blood of sprinkling,” the phrase names the atoning blood of Christ applied to the believer.
roots_lines: Blood of Sprinkling — Greek haima rhantismou, “blood of sprinkling.”
It is the atoning blood of Christ applied to the believer’s conscience.
It is contrasted with the blood of Abel, which cried for vengeance.
It speaketh better things, crying for pardon and peace.
By it the heart is sprinkled from an evil conscience.
usage: The blood of sprinkling speaketh better things than that of Abel, even pardon for the guilty.
Draw near with a true heart, having your heart sprinkled from an evil conscience.
Without shedding of blood is no remission; the conscience is purged by Christ alone.

etymology: From the Greek archegos kai teleiotes, “author and finisher,” or “leader and perfecter,” titles of Christ as the beginner and completer of the believer’s faith.
biblical_def: The Author and Finisher is a title of the Lord Jesus Christ, who both begins and perfects the faith of His people, set forth as the object on whom the runner of the race must fix his eye. Wherefore, having named the cloud of witnesses, the apostle says, Let us run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith (Heb 12:1; Heb 12:2). The dictionary marks both titles. As Author, Christ is the beginner and source of faith, for it is the gift of God; He is the captain of our salvation (Heb 2:10) who opens the path. As Finisher, He is the perfecter who will not leave His work undone, but performs it until the day of Jesus Christ (Php 1:6), bringing every believer through to glory. The pattern of His own endurance is set before us: who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame (Heb 12:2). So the Scripture teaches that the believer’s faith hangs not upon his own resolve, which would fail, but upon Christ who authored it and will surely finish it. This is the comfort of perseverance: not that the saint holds fast of his own strength, but that He who began the good work will complete it; and the eye of faith, looking unto Jesus, is kept from fainting because He who runs before is also He who carries through.
webster_summary: A title of Christ as the beginner and perfecter of the believer’s faith, on whom the runner of the race must look.
webster_full: AUTHOR AND FINISHER, a title of Christ as beginner and perfecter of faith.
As Author He is the source and beginner of faith, which is the gift of God.
As Finisher He perfects what He began, bringing every believer to glory.
He endured the cross, despising the shame, for the joy set before Him.
On Him the runner of the race must fix his eye, looking unto Jesus.

Heb 2:10
For it became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things, in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings.
corruption_summary: A glory of Christ little redefined; it recovers Him as the beginner and certain finisher of His people’s faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The Author and Finisher has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a beloved title in the preaching of perseverance. The dictionary records it that the reader may rest his hope not in the strength of his own believing but in the Christ who both begins and completes it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the perseverance of the saints, grounded not in the believer’s grip but in Christ’s. He is the Author who gives faith as His own gift, and the Finisher who will not leave His work undone, but performs it until the day of Jesus Christ. So the saint, looking unto Jesus, is kept from fainting in the race; for the same Lord who ran before, enduring the cross, carries His own through to the end. The eye of faith fixed on Him is the appointed means, but the finishing is His.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “author and finisher,” the title names Christ as beginner and perfecter of faith.
roots_lines: Author and Finisher — Greek archegos kai teleiotes, “leader and perfecter.”
As Author, Christ is the source and beginner of faith.
As Finisher, He perfects what He began unto glory.
He endured the cross for the joy set before Him.
On Him the runner of the race must fix his eye.
usage: Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith, the saint runs his race with patience.
He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.
The believer’s faith is begun and finished by Christ, not by his own resolve.

etymology: From the Greek nephos martyron, “cloud of witnesses,” the great company of the faithful of old who bear testimony to the life of faith.
biblical_def: The great cloud of witnesses is the host of the faithful saints of old, named and unnamed in the eleventh chapter of Hebrews, who having lived and died in faith bear testimony to the believer that the race may be run and won. Wherefore, says the apostle, seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us (Heb 12:1). The dictionary marks the figure rightly. These witnesses are not spectators in heaven peering down upon the saints below, as the unwary suppose, but witnesses in the older and truer sense: men who by their faith bore witness, who obtained a good report through faith (Heb 11:39), and whose recorded lives testify that God is faithful to them that trust Him. By faith Abel offered, by faith Enoch was translated, by faith Abraham obeyed; and all these, having obtained a good report, received not the promise, God having provided some better thing for us (Heb 11:40). So the Scripture sets them before the believer as a great host of testimony, that he run not as one alone but in the company of all the faithful who have proved the way. Their witness is an encouragement to lay aside every weight and to press on, looking past them to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, in whom alone the race is finished.
webster_summary: The great company of the faithful of old whose lives bear witness that the life of faith may be run and won.
webster_full: CLOUD OF WITNESSES, the host of the faithful saints of old.
They are the men of faith named in the eleventh chapter of Hebrews.
They are witnesses who bore testimony, not mere spectators in heaven.
They obtained a good report through faith and proved God faithful.
Their witness encourages the believer to lay aside every weight and run.

corruption_summary: A glory of the faith little redefined; it recovers the saints of old as witnesses by their faith, not spectators of ours.
corruption_paragraphs: The great cloud of witnesses has drawn little redefinition from the present age, though it is often read amiss, as if the dead watched the living from heaven. The dictionary records it that the reader may know these as witnesses in the truer sense, men whose faith bore testimony that God is faithful to them that trust Him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the faithful of old testify to us by their lives. They are not an audience of departed spirits but a host of witnesses who, by faith, obtained a good report; and their recorded endurance encourages the believer that the race may be run and won. So the saint runs not alone nor untried, but in the company of all who have gone before and proved the way, laying aside every weight and looking past them to Jesus, in whom alone the race is finished.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “cloud of witnesses,” the phrase names the faithful of old who bear testimony to faith.
roots_lines: Cloud of Witnesses — Greek nephos martyron, “cloud of witnesses.”
It is the host of the faithful saints named in Hebrews eleven.
They are witnesses by their faith, not spectators of ours.
They obtained a good report and proved God faithful.
Their witness encourages the believer to run with patience.
usage: Compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us run with patience the race set before us.
These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but embracing them afar off.
The saints of old testify by their faith that the race may be run and won.

etymology: From the Greek kreittonos anastaseos, “better resurrection,” the hope of the faithful tortured who looked beyond this life to the resurrection of the just.
biblical_def: The better resurrection is the hope set before the suffering saints, for which they endured torture rather than purchase a present deliverance by denying their God. The apostle, recounting the trials of the faithful, says, Women received their dead raised to life again: and others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection (Heb 11:35). The dictionary marks the comparison. Some women in the old time received their dead raised to life again, as the widow of Zarephath and the Shunammite by Elijah and Elisha; yet such restored ones must die again. But the martyrs looked for a better resurrection, the rising of the body unto eternal and incorruptible life, and so they accepted not the deliverance offered them at the price of apostasy, but endured the rack and the flame. For the Scripture teaches that there shall be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust (Act 24:15); but the resurrection of the just is the better, unto life everlasting, while the unjust awake to shame and everlasting contempt (Dan 12:2). It is this better resurrection that makes the saint bold to die, for he knows the trump shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible (1Co 15:52). So the believer is taught to weigh the light affliction of the present against the eternal weight of glory laid up in the resurrection of the just, and to choose, like the martyrs, the better thing.
webster_summary: The hope of the faithful tortured, who looked beyond a present deliverance to the resurrection of the just unto eternal life.
webster_full: BETTER RESURRECTION, the hope of the faithful tortured for their God.
Some women received their dead raised to life again, yet such must die anew.
The martyrs looked for the resurrection of the body unto eternal life.
They accepted not deliverance bought by denying their God.
It is the resurrection of the just, unto life everlasting and incorruption.

Dan 12:2
And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

And have hope toward God, which they themselves also allow, that there shall be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust.
corruption_summary: A glory of the gospel little redefined; it recovers the bodily resurrection of the just as the martyr’s sure hope.
corruption_paragraphs: The better resurrection has drawn little redefinition from the present age, though the hope of bodily resurrection is much neglected and sometimes thinned into a vague notion of the soul’s survival. The dictionary records it that the reader may hold the firm hope of the body raised incorruptible, which made the martyrs bold to die.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the bodily resurrection of the just unto eternal life. The faithful tortured looked not for a present deliverance, nor for the bare immortality of the soul, but for the rising of the body incorruptible at the last trump; and this hope was so weighty that they accepted not deliverance bought by denying their God. So the saint is taught to weigh the light affliction of the present against the eternal weight of glory laid up in the resurrection, and, like the martyrs, to choose the better thing.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “better resurrection,” the phrase names the martyr’s hope of the body raised unto eternal life.
roots_lines: Better Resurrection — Greek kreittonos anastaseos, “better resurrection.”
It is the hope of the faithful tortured for their God.
It is set above the raising of the dead who must die again.
It is the resurrection of the just unto eternal life.
It made the martyrs bold to endure the rack and the flame.
usage: Others were tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection.
The dead shall be raised incorruptible, and this corruptible shall put on incorruption.
The saint weighs present affliction against the glory of the resurrection of the just.

etymology: From the Greek sabbatismos, “a sabbath-keeping” or “sabbath rest,” the rest that remaineth to the people of God in Christ.
biblical_def: The rest that remaineth is the sabbath-rest laid up for the people of God, whereinto the believer enters by faith and shall enter fully in glory, ceasing from his own works as God did from His. There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God, says the apostle; for he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his (Heb 4:9; Heb 4:10). And he draws the warning: Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest, lest any man fall after the same example of unbelief (Heb 4:11). The dictionary marks the threefold rest the chapter sets forth. There was the rest of Canaan, into which Joshua led Israel; yet it could not have been the true rest, for David long after still spake of another day. There was the rest of God on the seventh day. And there is the rest that remaineth, the gospel rest in Christ, who says, Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Mat 11:28). So the Scripture teaches that the believer enters this rest now by faith, ceasing from his own works as the ground of acceptance and resting wholly upon Christ’s finished work; and that he shall enter it fully hereafter. The unbeliever, who hardens his heart, is shut out as the carcases fell in the wilderness; but to the faithful the rest remaineth sure, a sabbath that shall have no evening.
webster_summary: The sabbath-rest laid up for the people of God in Christ, entered now by faith and fully hereafter in glory.
webster_full: REST THAT REMAINETH, the sabbath-rest laid up for the people of God.
It is the gospel rest in Christ, who gives rest to the labouring and heavy laden.
The believer enters it by ceasing from his own works as God did from His.
It was foreshadowed by the rest of Canaan and the rest of the seventh day.
It is entered now by faith and fully hereafter, when the saint rests from his labours.

corruption_summary: A glory of the gospel little redefined; it recovers the believer’s rest in Christ’s finished work, entered by faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The rest that remaineth has drawn little redefinition from the present age, though rest is often hollowed out into mere leisure or inward calm apart from Christ. The dictionary records it that the reader may know it as the sabbath-rest in the finished work of Christ, ceasing from his own works as the ground of acceptance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is rest in the finished work of Christ. The believer enters this rest not by labour as a price, but by faith, ceasing from his own works as God ceased from His, and resting wholly upon what Christ hath done. Yet the apostle bids him labour to enter, lest he fall after the same example of unbelief; for the rest is entered by faith, and faith perseveres. To the faithful the rest remaineth sure, a sabbath that shall have no evening; the unbelieving are shut out, as the carcases fell in the wilderness.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “a sabbath-keeping,” the phrase names the rest that remaineth to the people of God in Christ.
roots_lines: Rest That Remaineth — Greek sabbatismos, “a sabbath-keeping.”
It is the gospel rest laid up for the people of God in Christ.
It was foreshadowed by Canaan’s rest and the rest of the seventh day.
The believer enters it by ceasing from his own works in faith.
It is entered now in part and fully hereafter in glory.
usage: There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God, a sabbath that shall have no evening.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.

etymology: From the Greek stephanos tes doxes, “crown of glory,” the unfading reward of grace laid up for the faithful at the appearing of Christ.
biblical_def: The crown of glory is the unfading reward of grace laid up for the faithful, given by Christ the chief Shepherd at His appearing. The apostle Peter, charging the elders to feed the flock willingly and not for filthy lucre, promises, And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away (1Pe 5:4). The dictionary marks this among the several crowns the Scripture sets before the believer: the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give at that day to all them also that love His appearing (2Ti 4:8); the crown of life, which the Lord hath promised to them that love Him (Jas 1:12); and here the crown of glory that fadeth not away. The figure is the garland given the victor in the games; but where the earthly crown withered in a day, this crown is incorruptible (1Co 9:25), a glory that never fades. So the Scripture teaches that the faithful shall not labour, nor suffer, nor watch over the flock in vain; for the chief Shepherd marks every labour of love, and will crown His own at His coming. Yet the crown is wholly of grace, given by the same Lord whose grace first wrought the faithfulness it rewards; and the redeemed shall cast their crowns before the throne (Rev 4:10), confessing that all the glory is His. So the believer endures, looking for the crown, and gives it back in worship to the Christ who won it for him.
webster_summary: The unfading reward of grace laid up for the faithful, given by Christ the chief Shepherd at His appearing.
webster_full: CROWN OF GLORY, the unfading reward laid up for the faithful.
It is given by Christ the chief Shepherd when He shall appear.
It stands among the crowns of righteousness and of life in Scripture.
The figure is the victor’s garland, but this crown fadeth not away.
The redeemed cast their crowns before the throne, ascribing all glory to Christ.

corruption_summary: A glory of the gospel little redefined; it recovers the believer’s reward as wholly of grace, cast back before the throne.
corruption_paragraphs: The crown of glory has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving in the funeral and the pulpit as the believer’s hope. The dictionary records it that the reader may know the crown as a reward of grace, not of merit, and as a glory laid up for the faithful at the appearing of Christ.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is reward wholly of grace. The crown is real, and the Scripture sets it before the faithful to stir them to endure; yet it is given by the same Lord whose grace first wrought the faithfulness it crowns, and the redeemed cast their crowns before the throne, confessing that all the glory is His. So the saint labours and suffers and watches over the flock not in vain, for the chief Shepherd marks every faithful work; and he looks for the crown that fadeth not away, only to give it back in worship to the Christ who won it for him.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “crown of glory,” the phrase names the unfading reward of grace for the faithful.
roots_lines: Crown of Glory — Greek stephanos tes doxes, “crown of glory.”
It is the unfading reward given by Christ the chief Shepherd.
It stands with the crowns of righteousness and of life.
It is the victor’s garland, yet incorruptible and never fading.
The redeemed cast their crowns before the throne in worship.
usage: When the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.
Blessed is the man that endureth temptation, for he shall receive the crown of life.

etymology: From the Greek theou zelos, “jealousy of God,” the holy zeal that guards the purity of God’s people for Christ their husband.
biblical_def: Godly jealousy is the holy zeal, modelled upon the jealousy of God Himself, by which a faithful pastor guards the purity of Christ’s people for Christ their husband. The apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians, For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ (2Co 11:2). The dictionary marks the distinction between this and the sinful jealousy of envy. Carnal jealousy is a work of the flesh (Gal 5:20), a grudging of another’s good; but godly jealousy is a fruit of love, a zeal for the honour of the beloved. So the LORD reveals Himself as a jealous God (Exo 20:5), not with the petty envy of men, but with the holy zeal of a husband who will not share His glory with another. Paul, set as the friend of the bridegroom, fears lest, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so their minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ (2Co 11:3). The dictionary commends godly jealousy as the proper affection of every faithful soul: a holy fear of any rival to Christ that would draw the bride from her one husband. So the Scripture teaches that love for Christ is rightly jealous; that to be at ease while error courts the church is no virtue but a failure of love; and that the truest tenderness toward God’s people is the zeal that keeps them chaste unto Christ alone.
webster_summary: The holy zeal, modelled on God’s own jealousy, that guards the purity of Christ’s people for Christ their husband.
webster_full: GODLY JEALOUSY, the holy zeal that guards God’s people for Christ.
It is modelled on the jealousy of God, who will not share His glory with another.
It differs from carnal jealousy, which is a work of the flesh.
Paul was jealous over the church to present her a chaste virgin to Christ.
It is the proper affection of every faithful shepherd and soul.
scriptures: For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.
But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.
Exo 20:5

Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;
For thou shalt worship no other god: for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God:
corruption_summary: A holy affection little redefined; it recovers jealousy as the zeal of love that keeps the church chaste unto Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Godly jealousy has drawn little redefinition from the present age, though jealousy as a word is now reckoned wholly a vice, so that the holy sense is forgotten. The dictionary records it that the reader may distinguish the carnal jealousy of envy from the godly jealousy of love, which guards the beloved’s honour.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that love for Christ is rightly jealous. The LORD calls Himself a jealous God, not with the petty envy of men but with the holy zeal of a husband who will not share His bride with idols; and the faithful pastor, as the friend of the bridegroom, is jealous over the church to keep her chaste unto Christ alone. So the saint is taught that to be at ease while error courts the church is no virtue but a failure of love, and that the truest tenderness toward God’s people is the zeal that guards them from every rival to their one husband.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “jealousy of God,” the phrase names the holy zeal that guards the church for Christ.
roots_lines: Godly Jealousy — Greek theou zelos, “jealousy of God.”
It is the holy zeal modelled on God’s own jealousy.
It differs from carnal jealousy, which is a work of the flesh.
It guards the church to present her a chaste virgin to Christ.
It is the proper affection of every faithful shepherd and soul.
usage: I am jealous over you with godly jealousy, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.
The LORD, whose name is Jealous, will not share His glory with another.
Godly jealousy is the zeal of love that keeps the church chaste unto Christ alone.

etymology: From the Greek skolops te sarki, “a stake” or “thorn for the flesh,” the affliction given Paul to keep him humble, in which God’s grace was made sufficient.
biblical_def: The thorn in the flesh is the affliction given to the apostle Paul, which God would not remove, that the apostle might be kept humble and that the power of Christ might rest upon his weakness. Lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, he writes, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me (2Co 12:7). The dictionary marks the wonder of the providence. The thorn was at once a messenger of Satan to buffet him and a gift given to him of God; for the same affliction that Satan meant for the apostle’s harm, God ordained for his good, even as Joseph said of his brethren’s evil, God meant it unto good (Gen 50:20). Thrice the apostle besought the Lord that it might depart from him; but the answer came not in removal but in sustaining grace: My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:9). So the Scripture teaches that God does not always lift the affliction He could lift, but gives instead a grace that is sufficient, and turns the very weakness into the seat of Christ’s power; that the unanswered prayer for removal is answered the better way; and that the thorn left in the flesh, sanctified, keeps the saint low at the foot of the cross, where the strength of Christ is perfected in him.
webster_summary: The affliction given Paul, which God would not remove, that His grace might be sufficient and Christ’s power perfected in weakness.
webster_full: THORN IN THE FLESH, the affliction given the apostle Paul.
It was a messenger of Satan to buffet him, given lest he be exalted.
It was at once Satan’s instrument and God’s gift for his good.
Thrice he besought the Lord, but it was not removed.
The answer was sustaining grace: My grace is sufficient for thee.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong.
But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
corruption_summary: A trial of the believer little redefined; it recovers the sufficiency of grace in unremoved affliction and the strength perfected in weakness.
corruption_paragraphs: The thorn in the flesh has drawn little redefinition from the present age, though much vain speculation is spent on what the thorn was, while its lesson is passed over. The dictionary records it that the reader may learn not the name of the thorn, which God hid, but the sufficiency of grace, which God revealed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sufficiency of grace in unremoved affliction. God does not always lift the affliction He could lift, but gives instead a grace that is sufficient, and turns the very weakness into the seat of Christ’s power. The thorn was Satan’s messenger and God’s gift at once, for the same evil Satan meant for harm God ordained for good. So the saint is taught that the unanswered prayer for removal may be answered the better way, and that the thorn left in the flesh, sanctified, keeps him low at the foot of the cross, where Christ’s strength is perfected in him.

etymology: From the Hebrew almanuth and Greek chera, “a widow,” the estate of her whose husband is dead, honoured of God and cared for by His church.
biblical_def: Widowhood is the estate of the woman whose husband is dead, an estate which Scripture marks with peculiar honour and peculiar care, for the LORD is the judge of the widow and the father of the fatherless (Psa 68:5). The apostle Paul charges the church to honour widows that are widows indeed (1Ti 5:3), and draws the portrait of such a one: she that is a widow indeed, and desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day (1Ti 5:5). The dictionary marks both the honour and the duty. The widow indeed, left desolate of earthly stay, casts herself wholly upon God, and her widowhood becomes a school of prayer and of trust, as it was with Anna, who departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day (Luk 2:37). And the church is charged to relieve such. So the Scripture teaches that pure religion and undefiled before God is this, to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction (Jas 1:27). The widow is no forgotten figure, but a charge laid upon the people of God, and a witness of faith that leans on no arm of flesh but on the LORD alone. Her trust in the day of desolation is set before the church as a pattern, and her relief as a sacred duty, that the bond of love in the body of Christ be kept, and the honour due the widow indeed be rendered her.
webster_summary: The estate of the woman whose husband is dead, honoured of God and given into the church’s sacred care.
webster_full: WIDOWHOOD, the estate of the woman whose husband is dead.
Scripture marks it with peculiar honour and peculiar care.
The widow indeed, left desolate, trusteth in God and continueth in prayer.

Pure religion is to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction.
scriptures: Now she that is a widow indeed, and desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day.
Honour widows that are widows indeed.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Luk 2:37
And she was a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day.
corruption_summary: An honoured estate now devalued; it recovers the honour of the widow indeed and the church’s sacred care for her.
corruption_paragraphs: Widowhood has drawn little open redefinition, yet the present age has quietly devalued the honoured estate of the widow, reckoning her affliction a private misfortune rather than a charge upon the people of God, and esteeming her trust in God a thing of weakness rather than of faith. The Scripture sets a higher mark, naming the widow indeed a woman of honour, whose desolation drives her to God and whose prayers ascend night and day.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour of the widow indeed and the church’s care for her. The widow is no forgotten figure, but a charge laid upon the people of God, and a witness of faith that leans on no arm of flesh but on the LORD alone. As Anna served God with fastings and prayers night and day, so the widow indeed continues in supplication, and the church is bound to honour and relieve her; for pure religion is to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction. So the bond of love in the body of Christ is kept, and the honour due the widow indeed is rendered her.
